title: Nigeria 2020 electricity tariff rise under World Bank power loan
point: Abuja, seat of the federal government and the electricity regulator NERC; the tariff rise applied nationwide

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Approved a US$750 million IDA credit, the Power Sector Recovery Operation, on 23 June 2020. Money is paid out only when agreed results are met. One required result (DLI #3) is that end-user tariffs are adjusted in line with a plan to remove tariff shortfalls. A separate US$500 million distribution-sector programme was approved in February 2021, and additional financing in June 2023.

conditions: World Bank Program-for-Results loan (P164001). Two 'global' results must be met before money for any other result is paid: the regulator sets company revenue needs through tariff reviews, and the government approves and carries out a financing plan to fully cover tariff shortfalls. Standard result DLI #3 requires end-user tariffs to be adjusted in line with that plan, including its measures to protect the poor. The 2023 additional financing ties later tariff reviews to keeping the social tariff for households using under 50 kWh a month (World Bank project paper, 2023).
community: In 2019 tariffs covered only 56% of cost, and the shortfall was ₦581 billion (US$1.6 billion). A July 2020 tariff review planned a 46% rise from September 2020; a 38% rise took effect in November 2020. By February 2022 tariffs reached 96.4% of cost (World Bank, 2023). The Bretton Woods Project, citing Nairametrics, said most Nigerians would pay more for power, in a year when the economy shrank 6.1% in the second quarter. In September 2020 the government also cut petrol subsidies (Reuters).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: The Nigeria Labour Congress called an indefinite general strike over the petrol and power price rises, to start on 28 September 2020. Reuters reported that Nigeria faced pressure for reforms from lenders such as the World Bank 'to qualify for budget support loans.' The unions suspended the strike after the government agreed to hold off the tariff rise for two weeks while a joint committee headed by Festus Keyamo, Minister of State for Labour and Employment, reviewed it. The 38% rise then took effect in November 2020. The World Bank calls that rise the main reason tariffs neared full cost.

Nigeria Power Sector Recovery Operation

confidence_note: The World Bank's own project paper ties loan payments to tariff adjustments and counts the 38% rise as a result. The size of the rise per household is not given in these sources.
check_note: Corrected the 50 kWh social tariff (a 2023 additional-financing condition, not a 2020 one), named the 2021 package as a separate distribution programme, and attributed the 'pay more' line to Nairametrics as cited by Bretton Woods Project. Changed 'ended' petrol subsidies to 'cut' and gave Keyamo's correct title.

title: Nigeria port concessions and dock job cuts
point: Apapa, Lagos, Nigeria's main port (approximate; the concessions covered ports nationwide)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its Privatization Support Project (IDA credit, US$114.29 million, approved June 2001, closed December 2009) supported the port reform. The World Bank lists port concessions (US$115 million in proceeds) among the privatizations achieved, with 24 port terminals concessioned.

conditions: Privatization Support Project: advisory and institutional support to the Bureau of Public Enterprises for privatizations and concessions, including the ports (World Bank completion report, 2011).
community: The World Bank's own completion report records that over 5,000 Nigerian Ports Authority staff were 'disengaged', with over ₦20 billion paid in entitlements, severance and pension buyouts. It estimates NPA staff fell from 13,146 to about 8,146, a 39% decline. Casual dock labourers were cut from about 13,000 to about 3,000. The report calls labour retrenchment probably the most difficult part of the port reform.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the source.
outcome: The World Bank counts shorter ship waiting times (from 14-21 days to 0-1 day) as gains. It says the port reform served as a model for Sierra Leone and Liberia.

sources.title: Nigeria - Privatization Support Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report

confidence_note: Only one source, the lender's own report, gives the job figures. Concession holders are not named in it.
check_note: Dates changed to the project's 2001-2009 span, since the report gives no concession dates. Added the report's NPA staff decline (13,146 to about 8,146) and narrowed the 'model' claim to Sierra Leone and Liberia as the report states.

title: Maputo water lease (Águas de Moçambique)
point: Maputo, centre of the 15-year lease area (management contracts also covered Beira, Quelimane, Nampula and Pemba)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: IDA credit 3247 for the Second National Water Development Project (1999) required the lease and management contracts to be signed before the credit could take effect, and set a full-cost-recovery tariff policy as a key indicator. IDA added a US$15 million supplemental credit in 2004 to cover higher contract costs.

conditions: Development Credit Agreement, Section 6.01(e): a condition for the credit to take effect was that the asset fund FIPAG had signed 'the Lease Contract and the Management Contract' with the winning bidder for Maputo, Beira, Quelimane, Nampula and Pemba (World Bank, 1999). A key project indicator was a tariff policy based on full cost recovery (World Bank completion report, 2009).

companies.name: SAUR International
companies.role: Lead shareholder of the operator Águas de Moçambique; left the contracts on 14 December 2001 and offered its share to Águas de Portugal for €1. HQ is its current head office.

companies.name: Águas de Portugal
companies.role: Second shareholder of the operator; took SAUR's share after SAUR left.

community: The World Bank expected customers with existing connections to pay higher tariffs. After SAUR left, the contracts were renegotiated: the operator's rate for Maputo rose and costs went up by about US$8.5 million, plus about US$7.15 million to cover operating deficits in four cities. A 2006 assessment found the share of peri-urban Maputo residents supplied by the operator fell from about 86% (2001) to 63% (2006). The share relying on small private providers, who charge much higher prices, doubled. The operator was persistently late paying lease fees to the public asset fund FIPAG.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: New contracts took effect in June 2004. Connections in Maputo rose from 77,793 (2000) to 109,932 (2009). FIPAG drew on the operator's US$400,000 security in December 2007 over unpaid fees. The World Bank rated the project's implementation unsatisfactory four times, until mid-2003, after SAUR's exit.

title: Kazakhstan pension privatization
point: Almaty, the capital when the 1997 pension law was passed (national measure)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Pension Reform Adjustment Loan (PRAL), US$300 million in three tranches, effective June 1998, with 19 conditions before Board approval, 8 for the second tranche and 9 for the third. It supported the move from a pay-as-you-go system to private individual accounts. The third tranche was cancelled for two unmet conditions.

conditions: The PRAL supported the June 1997 pension law that replaced the state pay-as-you-go system with fully funded individual accounts (10% of earnings), held in a state accumulation fund or private pension funds, and set tranche conditions on its implementation (World Bank President's Report, 1998; IEG evaluation, 2007). A parallel Asian Development Bank loan (US$100 million, approved December 1997) had 41 policy conditions, including enrolling at least 60% of those employed in the formal sector.
community: The replacement rate (pension as a share of pay) fell from 60% before the reform to 29.3% in 2013. Coverage fell from about 66% of the labour force to 63%. Fees were estimated to take 16.8% of an account's final balance after 40 years (ILO, 2018). A World Bank study projected replacement rates of about 23% for women and just over 40% for men (Asian Development Bank completion report). The retirement age was raised from 60 to 63 for men and 55 to 58 for women. The IMF estimated the 1998-2025 transition cost at 36.5% of 1997 GDP (cited by ILO, 2018).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: In 2013 Kazakhstan moved all members into a public Unified Pension Fund; the ILO lists Kazakhstan (2013) among countries that reversed pension privatization. The World Bank's own evaluation says the accounts are unlikely to give adequate pensions to many people, especially women and those with broken careers.

title: Bolivia 1997 pension privatization
point: La Paz, seat of government (national measure)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its Capitalization Program Adjustment Credit (CPAC) made approval of a pension law a condition for releasing the financial-sector tranche. A parallel Inter-American Development Bank loan had identical conditions. The Bank also financed studies in 1992 for a funded pension system.

conditions: CPAC tranche conditions included '(i) approval of a pension law providing for reform of the existing funds' and setting up accounts to distribute shares from the capitalization (sale) of state firms (World Bank IEG Bolivia evaluation, 2007).
community: Coverage stayed at about 12% of the labour force, the lowest in Latin America. Pensions averaged about 20% of average working-life pay. The share of older women receiving any pension fell from 23.7% to 12.8% between 1995 and 2007. Administrative costs were about 18% of contributions in 2004. Transition costs were 2.5 times the first estimates (ILO, 2018).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: Law No. 065 of 10 December 2010 replaced the private system with a public pay-as-you-go system for new entrants (ILO, 2018).

title: Oltchim privatization and insolvency

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: A draft letter of intent agreed with the IMF in May 2011 committed Romania to sell Oltchim, with a tender by end-2011 and liquidation if the sale failed (Ziarul Financiar). An earlier draft, reported by Mediafax in February 2011, set the sale for the second half of 2012. In January 2013 an IMF delegation warned the government must take urgent measures to avoid Oltchim's bankruptcy (Radio Romania International).

conditions: Draft IMF letter of intent (agreed 3 May 2011): appoint a legal adviser by end-June 2011 and an investment bank by end-September 2011, complete the tender by end-2011; if the sale failed by end-2011, 'the firm will be placed in liquidation' (Ziarul Financiar). The state owned 54.79% (Mediafax).
community: The 2012 privatization was won by businessman Dan Diaconescu, who did not pay the €45 million he pledged. Workers' pay was delayed in the last months of 2012. In March 2013 over 1,000 workers protested over unpaid wages, and the day before about 500 workers from Oltchim and its petrochemical division blocked traffic in Râmnicu Vâlcea and Pitești. Debt exceeded €620 million at the end of 2012 (Romania Insider).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: A court in Râmnicu Vâlcea approved insolvency on 30 January 2013. Romania Insider, citing unnamed sources, reported the prime minister concluded after talks with the IMF that insolvency was the main way to ease a sale. Layoffs were planned as part of restructuring.

title: Nicaragua BANADES closure and farm credit cuts
point: Managua, where the national development bank BANADES was based (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Under the 1998-2002 ESAF loan the IMF required the National Development Bank to be wound down and directed credit to end (Acevedo, Envío 2008). Envío (1998) reports the IMF demanded BANADES be privatized or closed and that Central Bank credit to it be cut off.

conditions: ESAF 1998-2002 (as listed by Envío, 2008): 'Liquidate at least 80% of the National Development Bank's assets'; also no use of directed credit policies and privatization of the grain agency ENABAS. The 1998 letter of intent promised to cancel BANADES' licence as a financial intermediary and to create a fund to finance bank branches, cooperatives and NGOs that lend in rural areas. Nicaragua's January 1999 letter of intent to the IMF confirms BANADES 'was liquidated' in June 1998.
community: BANADES, the country's oldest bank (85 years), served more than 80,000 producers in 1990 and fewer than 7,000 in 1997. Bank financing of farming fell from $92.4 million (1990) to $64.5 million (1996). State bank credit covered about 30,000 acres of beans and 88,300 acres of corn in 1990; in 1997 the state financed under 800 acres of beans and 5,800 acres of corn. Envío counted about 300,000 producers without financing (Rocha, Envío, March 1998). Acevedo notes more than 75% of farm jobs are in very small units with little land.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: The Ministry of Agriculture set up a Peasant Credit Fund to replace BANADES, lending through NGOs and cooperatives. Envío (1998) says President Alemán later announced he would use what was left of BANADES to create a state institution for peasants, which went back on the IMF commitment. The IMF agreement said farm credit policies 'were eliminated and will not be reintroduced'.

title: El Salvador 2025 public wage bill cuts and dismissals
point: San Salvador, capital (approximate); dismissals were spread across ministries, hospitals and town halls

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Extended Fund Facility (EFF) loan. Its first review (IMF Country Report 25/190) credits the early 2025 adjustment to 'visible cuts in the wage bill' and sets a civil service reform benchmark.

conditions: Program fiscal adjustment relying on wage bill cuts (IMF Country Report 25/190, July 2025), with a structural benchmark for a civil service reform plan; the reform aims to avoid unnecessary growth in public employment and cut the wage bill by about 1.5% of GDP by 2027. El Mundo reports the government committed to the IMF to cut wage bill spending by 0.8% of GDP in 2025, 1.3% in 2026 and 1.6% in 2027.
community: The Movement of Dismissed Workers (MTD) counted 17,810 public dismissals in 2025 by September, including 11,200 posts removed in the 2025 budget, 4,214 teacher posts at the Education Ministry cut or forced into retirement, 1,100 staff at the health fund Fosalud, 490 at the San Salvador Este town hall (340 in waste collection) and 83 doctors at the social security institute ISSS (El Mundo, September 2025).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: The MTD called the dismissals arbitrary and illegal and expected a new wave as new bodies such as ANDRES, the markets directorate and the new hospital network were set up. The IMF Board completed the first review on 27 June 2025; a civil service reform proposal is due by mid-2026 and a pension reform in early 2026.

title: Lebanon 2022 electricity tariff rise
point: Beirut, seat of the state utility Électricité du Liban (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Executive Magazine reports World Bank financing for Egyptian gas and Jordanian power imports (about $200 million for the Jordan deal) depended on conditions, one of which required EDL to raise electricity bills. The financing was not delivered.

conditions: Raise EDL electricity tariffs as a condition of proposed World Bank financing for gas and power imports (Executive Magazine, 2024). The IMF's April 2022 staff-level agreement also called for cost-recovery plans in the energy sector, without naming a tariff level.
community: On 1 November 2022 EDL raised tariffs from about 1 US cent per kWh to 10 cents for the first 100 kWh and 27 cents above that (The New Arab). By January 2024 EDL supply covered three to six hours a day on average (Executive Magazine). In a survey of 1,209 households, Human Rights Watch found nearly nine in ten said the cost of electricity hurt their ability to pay for other essentials; the poorest fifth went without power 11 hours a day on average.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: Executive Magazine reports EDL failed the World Bank's bill-collection requirement, and the import deals did not go ahead. Human Rights Watch urged the IMF to press Lebanon not to raise tariffs until it could guarantee reliable supply.

confidence_note: Only one source (Executive Magazine) states the World Bank required higher bills; The New Arab mentions only donor nations, and officials said the rise would pay for more fuel and raise supply to up to 10 hours a day. The World Bank financing was never delivered. HRW's survey also collected private generator bills, so its cost figures are not limited to the EDL tariff.
